props.title: Romeo + Juliet

sections.content: Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet revolutionized Shakespeare adaptation with its MTV-era aesthetic and fierce contemporary energy. Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes ignite the screen as star-crossed lovers in a neon-drenched Verona Beach, where gang warfare replaces family feuds and guns bearing the brand "Sword" stand in for rapiers. The film follows West Side Story (1961) in modernizing the classic tale, but Luhrmann's hyperkinetic style - rapid cuts, pop soundtrack, and baroque imagery - created a wholly new visual language for classical adaptation.

sections.content: The film's innovative approach to Shakespearean language - keeping the original text while setting it in contemporary America - influenced a wave of modern Shakespeare adaptations. 10 Things I Hate About You (1999) transported The Taming of the Shrew to high school, while O (2001) reimagined Othello in the world of prep school basketball. Luhrmann's visual excess and pop culture collision approach became a template for making classical texts accessible to young audiences without compromising their literary integrity.

The film's production design by Catherine Martin merges Catholic iconography, Miami crime aesthetics, and Shakespearean theatrical traditions into a cohesive visual feast. This approach influenced later genre-bending period pieces like Marie Antoinette (2006) and The Great Gatsby (2013), both of which use contemporary music and modern sensibilities to reinvigorate historical narratives. sections.content: The success of Romeo + Juliet sparked a renaissance in teen-oriented literary adaptations. Cruel Intentions (1999) reimagined Les Liaisons Dangereuses in upper-class Manhattan, while She's the Man (2006) turned Twelfth Night into a soccer comedy. These films followed Luhrmann's blueprint of maintaining sophisticated themes while packaging them in youth-friendly aesthetics.
